justice: The street mainly allocates space to mixed motor traffic in the center, while no clearly protected pedestrian or cycling zone is visible.
Shopfront spill-out objects such as stools, buckets, outdoor equipment and parked scooters occupy the edge space along both sides, reducing equal access for different users.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or barrier-free sidewalk features can be identified, limiting accessibility for users with mobility or sensory needs.
safety: There is no clear separation between pedestrians, cyclists, parked vehicles and moving cars, creating conflict risk in the narrow shared carriageway.
Several cars are parked along the right edge and scooters are parked near storefronts on the left, which can block sightlines and force people into vehicle space.
A pedestrian is walking in the middle of the roadway, indicating insufficient dedicated walking infrastructure and elevated exposure to traffic.
livability: Continuous ground-floor shops and restaurants on both sides provide everyday services and support street activity.
The two-story commercial buildings create an active mixed-use environment that can meet basic local needs within short distance.
However, the street lacks visible public amenities such as benches, street trees, or social resting spaces, which limits broader day-to-day livability.
sustainability: No visible street trees, planting strips, or green infrastructure are present, indicating weak ecological performance and little stormwater or shade support.
The street design appears oriented toward cars and curbside parking rather than clearly prioritizing walking, cycling, or public transport.
No visible bus stop, bike parking area, or dedicated bicycle lane can be identified to support lower-carbon travel choices.
aesthetics: The repeated two-story building form on both sides creates some visual order and enclosure.
Colorful commercial signs add local character and make the street feel active rather than empty.
At the same time, exposed air-conditioning units, cluttered storefront edges, parked vehicles, and limited greenery reduce overall visual quality.
comfort: There is almost no visible tree canopy or shading device over the street, so thermal comfort is likely poor in hot weather.
The road surface appears mostly even, but there is no clear protected pedestrian walkway, reducing physical comfort for people on foot.
Storefront clutter, parked scooters, and close interaction with moving vehicles can create psychological discomfort for all users.
No benches or dedicated resting facilities are visible along the commercial frontage.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is clearly visible; pedestrians appear to share space directly with cars in the carriageway.
There are no marked crosswalks, pedestrian refuge areas, or curb extensions visible along this segment.
Active shopfronts can make the route more interesting to walk along, but walking quality is undermined by parked vehicles and edge obstructions.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, painted cycle marking, or physical protection for cyclists is visible anywhere on the street.
Cyclists would need to ride in mixed traffic with cars and alongside parked vehicles, increasing dooring and overtaking risk.
No visible bicycle parking racks or cycling-support facilities are provided near the shops.
